The word "log" has three separate, unrelated meanings as a noun. Each belongs to a completely different context. Here they all are, one by one.

The most basic meaning of "log" is a thick, heavy piece of wood cut from a tree.

When a tree is chopped down or falls, its long trunk is usually cut into shorter, roughly cylindrical pieces. Each of those pieces is a log. Think of it like slicing a long baguette of bread into shorter sections — except it's a tree trunk.

Key characteristics:

  • Comes from the trunk or a very thick branch of a tree
  • Usually still has bark on the outside
  • Solid, heavy, and roughly round in cross-section
  • Can range from a foot to many feet in length

What logs are used for:

  • Firewood — logs are split into smaller pieces and burned in fireplaces and campfires
  • Construction — a "log cabin" is a small house built by stacking logs on top of one another
  • Lumber — logs are taken to sawmills and cut into flat planks used to build furniture, houses, and floors
  • Paper — logs are ground into a wet pulp to make paper and cardboard

Common expressions using this meaning:

  • "Throw another log on the fire" — add a piece of wood to keep the fire burning
  • "Sleeping like a log" — sleeping so deeply that you are completely still and unresponsive, just like a log lying on the ground
  • "A log jam" — originally, a massive tangle of floating logs blocking a river; now also used to describe any situation that is completely stuck and not moving forward

The second meaning of "log" is a formal, chronological record of events, activities, or observations.

Think of it like a diary — but more factual, structured, and official. While a diary might include feelings and personal reflections, a log records what happened, when it happened, and sometimes who did it — with little to no personal commentary.

The key features of a log as a record:

  • Entries are written in chronological order, from earliest to most recent
  • Each entry is typically time-stamped — marked with the exact date and/or time it was recorded
  • The tone is factual and impersonal — it reports events, it does not reflect on them
  • It is maintained regularly or whenever something significant occurs
  • It is meant to be a reliable, permanent reference that others can read and trust

Why do people keep logs?

In many fields — shipping, aviation, medicine, science, computing — it is critical to have an accurate record of what happened and when. If something goes wrong, you can look back at the log and trace the exact sequence of events. If something needs to be proved or investigated, the log serves as evidence.

Types of logs and where they're found:

a) Ship's Log (or Captain's Log)
This is the most historically famous type of log. On a ship, the captain or officer on duty keeps a running record of the vessel's journey — its position, speed, direction, weather conditions, and any significant events such as storms, mechanical failures, or encounters with other ships. This log is kept continuously throughout the entire voyage.

You may recognize "Captain's log, stardate..." from Star Trek — that's a direct reference to this seafaring tradition.

b) Flight Log (Pilot's Logbook)
Pilots are legally required to maintain a personal logbook recording every flight they make — the date, the aircraft used, the route, the flight duration, and the conditions (day or night, weather type). This record tracks their experience and qualifications over a career.

c) Medical Log / Patient Chart
In hospitals, doctors and nurses record everything that happens to a patient — vital signs, medications given, treatments performed, and test results — all with timestamps. This is a type of log.

d) Call Log
A record of telephone calls — who called, when, and for how long. The "recent calls" screen on your phone is essentially a call log.

e) Computer / System Log
This is one of the most important modern uses of the word. In computing, a log (or log file) is an automatically generated record of everything that happens inside a computer system, application, or network.

For example:

  • A server log records every request made to a website — who visited, which page they viewed, when, and from where
  • An error log records every crash or failure that occurs in a software program
  • A security log records login attempts and access events

System logs are essential for debugging (finding and fixing problems), security monitoring, and understanding how a system is behaving.

f) Other common types:

  • Activity log — a record of what actions were taken by a person or system
  • Maintenance log — a record of repairs and servicing done on a machine or vehicle
  • Work log — a record of hours worked and tasks completed

Common expressions using this meaning:

  • "Log it" — write it down in the official record
  • "According to the log..." — referring to the record as a source of evidence
  • "Keep a log" — maintain a regular written record of something

The third meaning is strictly mathematical. Here, "log" is simply a shortened form of the word logarithm.

To understand a logarithm, you first need to recall exponentiation — which you already know, even if you don't know the term. It just means raising a number to a power:

10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000
Written as: 10³ = 1,000
Read as: "10 raised to the power of 3 equals 1,000."

A logarithm reverses this question. Instead of asking "what do I get when I raise 10 to the power of 3?", a logarithm asks:

"If I start with 10 and I want to reach 1,000 — what power do I raise it to?"

The answer is 3. And we write this as:

log₁₀(1,000) = 3
Read as: "The log base 10 of 1,000 equals 3."

So a logarithm is the exponent. It tells you the power you need.

The three parts of a logarithm:

  • The base — the number being raised to a power (10 in the example above)
  • The argument — the number you're trying to reach (1,000 above)
  • The logarithm — the exponent that gets you there (3 above)

The most common bases used:

a) Log base 10 — the Common Logarithm

When you see "log" written without a base specified:

log(1,000) = 3

...it almost always means log base 10. This is called the common logarithm.

More examples:

  • log(10) = 1, because 10¹ = 10
  • log(100) = 2, because 10² = 100
  • log(10,000) = 4, because 10⁴ = 10,000
  • log(1) = 0, because 10⁰ = 1

Notice something powerful here: as the number grows by a factor of 10 (from 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000), the logarithm only increases by 1. This is what makes logarithms so useful — they compress enormous numbers into small, manageable ones.

b) Log base e — the Natural Logarithm (ln)

There is a special number in mathematics called e, approximately equal to 2.718. It appears naturally in many areas of science and mathematics (hence the name "natural"). Logarithms using this base are called natural logarithms and are written as ln, not "log". They appear constantly in calculus, physics, biology, finance, and engineering.

c) Log base 2 — the Binary Logarithm

Used extensively in computer science, since computers operate in binary (base 2). Written as log₂.

  • log₂(2) = 1, because 2¹ = 2
  • log₂(4) = 2, because 2² = 4
  • log₂(8) = 3, because 2³ = 8
  • log₂(1,024) = 10, because 2¹⁰ = 1,024

Why are logarithms so useful in the real world?

Many phenomena in nature and human life don't grow or change in straight lines — they grow or change in dramatic, multiplying leaps. Logarithms allow us to handle these enormous ranges by compressing them into a neat, readable scale.

  • Earthquakes (Richter scale): The scale is logarithmic. An earthquake of magnitude 7 is not slightly stronger than magnitude 6 — it is 10 times more powerful. Magnitude 8 is 100 times more powerful than magnitude 6.
  • Sound (Decibel scale): The decibel scale is logarithmic. A 30-decibel increase doesn't mean the sound is 30 units louder — it means it is 1,000 times more intense.
  • Acidity (pH scale): A liquid with pH 3 is 10 times more acidic than one with pH 4, and 100 times more acidic than one with pH 5.
  • Computer science: Algorithms are often measured by how their time or steps scale with input size. When an algorithm scales as log₂(n), it is extremely efficient — for example, searching through 1,000,000,000 items might only take about 30 steps.
  • Finance: Logarithms are used to model compound growth and calculate rates of return over time.

The word "log" as a noun has three completely unrelated meanings:

1. A log (piece of wood) — A heavy, roughly cylindrical section cut from a tree trunk. Used for fire, construction, or timber production.

2. A log (record) — A chronological, time-stamped, factual written record of events. Used on ships, in aviation, medicine, computing, and many other fields to maintain an accurate history of what happened and when.

3. A log (mathematics) — Short for "logarithm." It is the inverse of exponentiation — it tells you what exponent you need to raise a base number to in order to reach a given result. It is a core tool in science, engineering, computing, and anywhere humans need to handle very large or very rapidly changing quantities.

Context will always make it clear which meaning is intended — whether you're standing by a campfire, reading a ship's report, or working through a math problem.
